title: Rotate List
prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `k`, rotate the list to the right by `k` places and return the new head.

The list is given as an array (e.g. `[1,2,3,4,5]` represents `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null`). The starter code includes helpers to convert between the array and a linked-list node — build the actual list, rotate it by manipulating `next` pointers, then convert back to an array to return.

examples.explanation: k can be larger than the list length; only k % length rotations actually matter.
An empty list (allowed by the constraints) has nothing to rotate, so it stays empty regardless of k.

constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 500]
hints: k can be much larger than the list's length — the effective rotation only ever depends on k modulo the length.
If you connect the tail back to the head, the list becomes circular; rotating right by k then just means picking a new 'break point'.
Find the list's length first, compute k % length, then walk (length - k % length - 1) steps from head to find the new tail; the node after it is the new head. Break the circle there.

solution.approach: Compute the list length while finding the tail, then join tail.next to head to make the list circular — this makes any rotation just a matter of choosing where to 'cut' the circle. The effective rotation is k % length (rotating by the full length or a multiple of it changes nothing). The new tail sits at position (length - k % length - 1) from the original head; walking there and breaking the next pointer right after it produces the rotated list starting at the following node.
